traveler: José Gabriel Condorcanqui Noguera, Túpac Amaru II
title: The Three Villages and the Four Quarters: the Curaca of Tungasuca, the Rising of 1780, and the Body Sent to Six Towns
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Surimana, the birth in the province of Canas
stops.date_confidence: contested: es.wikipedia gives 19 March 1738, en.wikipedia c. 1742; both report a baptism on 1 May, four years apart. No parish register is reachable to close the gap.
stops.campa: In a curacazgo village of the province of Canas, high on the Apurimac side of the cordillera, a son is born to the cacique Miguel Condorcanqui and Rosa Noguera. They name him Jose Gabriel. The house he is born into holds three villages by inheritance, Surimana, Pampamarca and Tungasuca, and holds them under a crown that has ruled these valleys for two hundred years. The family tells him he descends from the Inca the Spanish beheaded in Cusco's plaza in 1572. The claim is a story long before it is ever a lawsuit, and he is told it early.
suggested_refs: The parish register of Surimana, unlocated, which would settle the 1738 or 1742 question

stops.name: Cusco, the orphan taken in
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the sources say only that his parents died when he was about twelve. No year, month or day is recorded.
stops.campa: His parents die while he is still a boy, and an aunt and uncle take him north to Cusco. The city he enters is the old Inca capital wearing Spanish stone: Dominican walls set on Qorikancha's masonry, a cathedral on the square where his claimed ancestor was put to death. No source records the aunt's name, the uncle's trade, or the street. He arrives a provincial heir whose first language is Quechua, and he will leave the city fluent in the language of the courts that later refuse him.
suggested_refs: Cusco notarial records of the 1750s, for the household that raised him

stops.name: Colegio San Francisco de Borja, the Latin of the caciques
stops.date_confidence: traditional: attendance is attested, but no enrollment or leaving date appears in any reachable source. The building also moved during the college's history, so a single pin simplifies.
stops.campa: The Jesuits keep a school in Cusco for the sons of caciques, where Andean noble heirs learn to read, to write, to construe Latin and to recite Christian doctrine alongside one another. Jose Gabriel is sent to it. He comes out with three languages, Spanish, Quechua and Latin, and with the particular knowledge the school exists to impart: how the empire words things. Spain built the college to make loyal intermediaries of the grandsons of its enemies. It works as designed for two centuries, and then it produces this one.
suggested_refs: Jesuit matriculation books of the Colegio San Francisco de Borja, Cusco

stops.name: Surimana, the marriage to Micaela Bastidas
stops.date_confidence: attested; the venue is corrected from Pampamarca, which is her birthplace, to the church of Surimana
stops.campa: In the church of Nuestra Senora de la Purificacion he marries Micaela Bastidas Puyucahua, born at Pampamarca sixteen years before, of Indigenous and Afro-descended parentage. She is not quite sixteen. She will hold the supply lines, sign the orders and write the letters that keep two provinces in the field, and her argument with him about Cusco will outlive nearly everything else the rebellion puts on paper. None of that is visible in 1760. For twenty years they are the family that governs three villages.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of the Iglesia de Nuestra Senora de la Purificacion, Surimana

stops.name: Tungasuca, the cacicazgo of three villages
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the confirmation year is given without month or day
stops.campa: He is confirmed curaca of Surimana, Pampamarca and Tungasuca, succeeding his father's line, and takes the seat at Tungasuca. With the office comes a herd of some three hundred and fifty mules and the trade they carry. A curaca in this century stands in a narrow place: he collects from his people the tribute the crown demands, and answers to his people for the crown that demands it. He holds the position fourteen years, and he rides the roads himself, so he knows load by load what the roads carry.
suggested_refs: Colonial confirmations of the cacicazgo of Surimana, Pampamarca and Tungasuca

stops.name: Potosi, the mule road and the mountain
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the muleteering years span the 1760s and 1770s. No single dated journey to Potosi survives.
stops.campa: The trade road runs south from Cusco across the altiplano to the silver mountain, and he runs mules on it. At the far end waits the mita, the labor draft that takes men from villages like his own by quota and sends them into the Cerro Rico to work seams that have been swallowing Andean conscripts for two hundred years. He watches the drafts go down the road and watches what comes back up it. The petitions he later files against the mita are argued in loads and quotas, the units of his own trade.
suggested_refs: Mita quota registers for the province of Canas, 1760s-1770s

stops.name: Lima, the Real Audiencia and the marquisate
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the litigation runs 1776 to 1780. The year of the Lima journey itself is not attested in any reachable source.
stops.campa: He travels to the viceregal capital to sue. The claim is that he is legitimate heir to the Marquisate of Oropesa by direct descent from Tupac Amaru, the Inca the Spanish beheaded in 1572, and it is argued in proper form before the Real Audiencia, with genealogies and notaries and fees. In the same years he petitions for his people to be released from tribute and from the mining draft. He loses the suit. The petitions go unanswered. He has used every remedy the empire offers, in its own forms and at his own expense, and holds nothing at the end of it.
sources: J. Fisher, 'Bourbon Peru' (2003), at second hand
suggested_refs: The Oropesa succession file before the Real Audiencia de Lima, 1776-1780

stops.name: Tinta, the corregidor's account book
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the reparto grievance runs continuously through the 1770s. 1778 is fixed as the year of the alcabala increase, not of any single event here.
stops.campa: The provincial capital stands on the Vilcanota, and in it sits the corregidor Antonio de Arriaga, who administers the reparto de mercancias: goods nobody asked for, sold to indigenous communities at his price, on his terms, collectable in his court. In 1778 the crown raises the alcabala on common goods and tightens collection. Two years before that it moved the silver revenue of these mountains toward Buenos Aires. The valley is being priced by three offices at once, and one of the three keeps its ledger here.
suggested_refs: Reparto accounts of the corregimiento of Tinta under Antonio de Arriaga

stops.name: Yanaoca, the corregidor seized
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A celebration is held for Charles III, and Arriaga rides to it. Condorcanqui and his men take him on the road afterward and put him under guard. The corregidor is not killed. He is held for days and made to write, in his own hand and under his own seal, orders drawing arms, money and men out of the provincial treasury toward the very people holding him. Almost everything the rising uses in its first month, the empire signs for. The sources count this day as the beginning of the war.
suggested_refs: The requisition orders extracted from Arriaga under guard, November 1780

stops.name: Tungasuca, the corregidor hanged
stops.date_confidence: attested; the older reading that made this the same event as the 4 November capture is a conflation, not a source dispute
stops.campa: In the plaza at Tungasuca, before a crowd of indigenous people, mestizos and criollos, Arriaga is hanged. The executioner is Antonio Oblitas, the corregidor's own slave, who will himself be killed in Cusco six months later. The cry raised here keeps the king and kills the government: death to bad government, long live the king, no more alcabala and no customs house. This is not yet a war against Spain. It is a war against the men Spain sends, conducted in the king's own name, and it does not stay that way for three weeks.
stops.quote: que muera el mal gobierno, viva el rey y no pague alcabala, ni aduana...
stops.quote_source: Proclamation formula reported at the execution of Antonio de Arriaga, Tungasuca, November 1780; quoted in several accounts, primary document not seen
suggested_refs: The judicial file on the execution of Antonio de Arriaga and of Antonio Oblitas

stops.name: Tungasuca, the bando de libertad
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Six days after the hanging he issues the bando. It abolishes the reparto de mercancias, the mita and the customs house, and it declares free the enslaved Africans and Afro-Peruvians of these provinces. Micaela Bastidas signs the orders that carry it out to the caciques, and the paper moves faster than any army he has. The bando makes its case from grievance: he has petitioned for years, the royal courts have produced no remedy, and so he acts in their place and says so in writing.
stops.quote: that there have been repeated outcries directed to me by the indigenous peoples of this and surrounding provinces, outcries against the abuses committed by European-born crown officials... Justified outcries that have produced no remedy from the royal courts
stops.quote_source: Proclamation of Tupac Amaru II, November 1780, issued after Arriaga's execution; English translation in Chambers and Chasteen, Latin American Independence (Hackett, 2010), 33-34
suggested_refs: The Spanish original of the November 1780 proclamation, known here only in English translation

stops.name: Pillpinto, the bridge and the women's battalion
stops.date_confidence: contested: es.wikipedia dates the Pillpinto action 16 November 1780, the English chronology 26 November 1780. Ten days apart, unresolved.
stops.campa: At the bridge at Pillpinto, Tomasa Tito Condemayta, cacica of Acos, holds the crossing with a battalion of women. What moves through these valleys is a coalition of caciques, each bringing the people he governs, and part of what they bring answers to women holding office in their own right. She will be taken with the others in April. She will be killed in the plaza at Cusco in May, before Micaela Bastidas, on the same scaffolding and within the same hour.
suggested_refs: Trial records of Tomasa Tito Condemayta, cacica of Acos

stops.name: Sangarara, the roof of the church
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A royalist militia column marches out from Cusco and is met at Sangarara. The fighting runs some six hours around midday. The royalists fall back into the church; the attackers fire what remains of the roof and it comes down on them. Counts of the dead run from three hundred and ninety-five bodies gathered afterward in the streets, plaza and church, up to five hundred and seventy-eight killed to a man. Bishop Moscoso y Peralta excommunicates him for the burning, and both sides cite Sangarara in every argument that follows.
suggested_refs: The excommunication issued by Bishop Juan Manuel Moscoso y Peralta after Sangarara

stops.name: Tungasuca, proclaimed Jose I
stops.date_confidence: contested: es.wikipedia gives 26 November 1780, but the primary manifesto page and its neighbour carry Tungasuca datelines of 15 and 16 November. The document is also titled a presumed manifesto by its own editors.
stops.campa: He takes the regnal name Jose I and the name of the executed Inca for his own, and the war changes shape. Until now the cry has kept the king and cursed his officers. The manifesto circulating under his name says something else: that the kings of Castile have held the crown and dominion of his people usurped for close to three centuries. Whether the paper is his, its modern editors will not say; they print it as presumed. What is certain is that from this month forward men address him as Inca.
stops.quote: los reyes de Castilla me han tenido usurpada la corona y dominio de mis gentes cerca de tres siglos
stops.quote_source: Presunto manifiesto de Tupac Amaru a la ciudadania, Congreso del Peru, La Rebelion de Tupac Amaru II, vol. 6, p. 161; the edition's own title marks the text as attributed, not certain
sources: Congreso del Peru, La Rebelion de Tupac Amaru II, vol. 6
suggested_refs: The manuscript behind the presunto manifiesto, whose authenticity its editors decline to vouch for

stops.name: Ayaviri, the road to the lake
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The rising moves south out of Canas toward Lake Titicaca, and Ayaviri falls in the first week of December. This is the direction he chooses over Cusco: the mining districts and the herding towns of the altiplano, where the mita quotas fall hardest and the villages are most nearly all indigenous. He is recruiting the population the draft has been taking. The choice gains him an army across two provinces and costs him the six weeks in which Cusco is least able to hold itself.
stops.quote: I have acted ... only against the mentioned abuses and to preserve the peace and well-being of Indians, mestizos, zambos, as well as native-born whites and blacks.
stops.quote_source: The same November 1780 proclamation quoted at Tungasuca, not a second document; English translation in Chambers and Chasteen, Latin American Independence (Hackett, 2010), 33-34
suggested_refs: Royalist correspondence on the fall of Ayaviri, December 1780

stops.name: Pisac, the column turned back
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: His cousin Diego Cristobal takes more than six thousand followers north into the Sacred Valley toward Paucartambo, meaning to close on Cusco from above while the main force works the south. Royalist troops break the column near the bridge at Pisac. The pincer never shuts. Diego Cristobal survives the defeat, and he will still be alive and still under arms two years after his cousin is dismembered, which is why the crown will eventually have to break an amnesty to be rid of him.
suggested_refs: Accounts of the action at the Pisac bridge, 8 December 1780

stops.name: Cusco, the camp at San Sebastian
stops.date_confidence: attested; the investment of the city runs roughly 2 to 10 January 1781, not from 20 December 1780, which is the day the army was ordered to march
stops.campa: The army comes up the valley at last and camps at San Sebastian, on the southeastern approach. Micaela Bastidas has been pressing for the assault for a month, in letters that do not soften: the city is thinly held, the moment is now, and every week spent recruiting in the south is a week Lima uses. He does not storm it. The garrison has put indigenous fighters in its front rank, and he will not buy Cusco by killing them. The reason is his own. The cost of it gets counted by everyone who writes about the siege afterward.
suggested_refs: The letters of Micaela Bastidas urging the immediate assault on Cusco

stops.name: Sacsayhuaman, the heights above the city
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the siege camp is not separately dated. It falls inside the roughly eight days the city was actually invested.
stops.campa: The siege camp sits on the high ground by the old fortress, where the walls of the Inca city still stand above the Spanish one. From here he can see the square he claims by descent and cannot enter. The investment lasts a little over a week. Inside, the criollos of Cusco do not rise for him and the loyalist caciques hold; outside, his own levies begin drifting home, as levies do, to fields that will not wait on a siege. The mountain gives him the view and gives him nothing else.
stops.quote: Solo siento de los paisanos criollos, a quienes ha sido mi ánimo no se les siga algún perjuicio, sino que vivamos como hermanos
stops.quote_source: Proclamation attributed to Tupac Amaru II, 1780, addressed to the criollos; quoted in es.wikipedia, occasion not independently fixed
sources: L. E. Fisher (1966), at second hand
suggested_refs: Royalist accounts of the siege camp above Cusco, January 1781

stops.name: Cusco, the assault at San Cristobal fails
stops.date_confidence: approximate: en.wikipedia ends the siege 11 January 1781, es.wikipedia 9 January. The final assault falls inside that window.
stops.campa: The columns come at the northern parishes, San Cristobal and San Sebastian, and are stopped there. Within a day or two he lifts the siege and withdraws south. The reinforcement he feared has not even arrived: the army from Lima, fifteen thousand strong and more, will not enter Cusco until the twenty-fourth of February, six weeks after he leaves. He besieged the city in the one window when it could be taken, held that window about eight days, and did not take it.
suggested_refs: The Cusco cabildo's record of the defense, January 1781

stops.name: Cusco, the army from Lima
stops.date_confidence: attested; this force did not defend the siege, which had been lifted six weeks earlier, a conflation common in summaries
stops.campa: The viceroy Agustin de Jauregui has been assembling a response since November, and it arrives: a punitive army under the field commander Jose del Valle and the visitador Jose Antonio de Areche, which will pass twenty thousand men. Areche is the crown's fiscal inspector rather than a soldier, sent to Peru to reform the collection of revenue, and it is his signature that ends this. The rising began over the ledgers he came to tighten. He will write the sentence on it himself, in his own office, in the language of an audit.
suggested_refs: Areche's commission as visitador general and his revenue instructions for Peru

stops.name: Combapata, cavalry in open ground
stops.date_confidence: attested; corrected from an earlier reading that dated this to March 1781 and treated it as a retreat waypoint rather than a pitched defeat
stops.campa: Del Valle brings him to battle on flat ground beside the Vilcanota, where cavalry and firearms settle the question against slings and captured muskets. The rebel army breaks. Condorcanqui goes into the river to get clear and comes out on the far bank alive, with the country between Tinta and Sangarara still full of his people. Checacupe falls the next day. He has one week left as a free man and he spends it among villages his family has governed for generations.
suggested_refs: Del Valle's campaign dispatches for Combapata and Checacupe, April 1781

stops.name: Langui, betrayed by his own officers
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the date; the exact point of seizure is genuinely disputed, with Ninamarca and the road toward Tinta also named, and the Langui district's own account carries no mention of it
stops.campa: Colonel Ventura Landaeta and Captain Francisco de la Cruz, officers of his own camp, take him and hand him over against promises of clemency. The accounts do not agree on the spot: Langui, or Ninamarca, or somewhere on the road toward Tinta. What they agree on is who did it. The army of twenty thousand that has marched after him since February never closes on him. Two men who had been eating at his fire hand him over instead, in exchange for terms.
suggested_refs: The clemency terms granted to Ventura Landaeta and Francisco de la Cruz

stops.name: Tinta, Micaela and the sons taken
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the days; the sources place the arrests in the Tinta and Langui district. The claim that they were fleeing toward La Paz is unsupported and is dropped.
stops.campa: Micaela Bastidas is taken in the same district within hours, with their sons Hipolito and Fernando. Through the winter she has run what the rebellion had in place of a state: requisitions, couriers, the letters to caciques that kept two provinces in the field, and the argument about Cusco that she lost. The family is together in one place for the first time in five months, and the place is a column of prisoners on the road north. Fernando is ten years old.
suggested_refs: The arrest inventory of the Condorcanqui-Bastidas household, April 1781

stops.name: Cusco, brought in chains
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of April the prisoners enter Cusco: Condorcanqui, his wife, his sons, his uncle, his brother-in-law, some thirty others, and Areche riding with them. The city he could not take in January receives him in irons through the same northern parishes his columns attacked. He is lodged and interrogated a few hundred paces from the square where his claimed ancestor was beheaded two centuries before, and where, in five weeks, the sentence will be carried out on him.
stops.quote: de qué me sirve que sea Tupa Amaro que no hemos de hacer algo por nuestros paisanos
stops.quote_source: Trial record compiled by the oidor Benito de la Mata Linares, Cusco, 1781; quoted in es.wikipedia
suggested_refs: The Cusco prison registers for the April 1781 intake of rebel prisoners

stops.name: Cusco, the record of the torment
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: They put him to the torture to get names, and a court scribe sits beside it writing down what he says. The document survives. It is not oratory and was never meant to be read: a man crying mercy, saying he is lost, saying there is nothing more, saying the word indios. Of everything attributed to him this is the least literary and the most certainly his, because the state produced it against him and had no reason to improve it. The names they want are not in it.
stops.quote: ay, ay, ay misericordia Señor...ay, ay, ya estoy perdido...ay, ay, nada más, no hay más, los indios
stops.quote_source: Diligencia de ejecucion del tormento, recorded by the scribe Manuel Espinavete Lopez, Cusco, 29 April 1781; quoted in es.wikipedia
suggested_refs: The full diligencia de ejecucion del tormento of 29 April 1781, seen here only in excerpt

stops.name: Cusco, Areche comes to the cell
stops.date_confidence: undated: the confrontation is placed in the Cusco cell before sentencing, but no day is recorded. The utterance is remembered in a memoir written decades later, not in the trial record.
stops.campa: The visitador comes down to the cell himself and offers the usual exchange: the names of the accomplices, and something less than the worst. What comes back is that there are no accomplices here except the two of them, the oppressor and the liberator, and that both deserve to die. It is remembered by his half-brother, who wrote it out in exile long afterward, and by no clerk. Whether he spoke those words in that room, the judicial record does not say and cannot be made to say.
stops.quote: aquí no hay más cómplices, que tú y yo; tú, por opresor, y yo, por libertador, merecemos la muerte
stops.quote_source: Las memorias de Juan Bautista Tupac Amaru, his half-brother, published 1825; Congreso del Peru, La Rebelion de Tupac Amaru, vol. 1, p. 728
sources: Congreso del Peru, La Rebelion de Tupac Amaru, vol. 1
suggested_refs: Las memorias de Juan Bautista Tupac Amaru (1825), the sole witness to this exchange

stops.name: Cusco, Areche writes the sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested; the text is known here only in English translation, the Spanish original not read
stops.campa: The sentence is written out in the flat administrative Spanish of a fiscal inspector, and it specifies the machinery: the tongue cut out, the limbs bound to four horses, the horses driven toward the four corners of the plaza. It then disposes of the parts afterward, town by town, so that the punishment can be seen in every valley that rose. Nothing in it is improvised. It comes from the same office and the same hand that were sent to Peru to make the accounts run properly.
stops.quote: ...to four horses who will then be driven at once toward the four corners of the plaza, pulling the arms and legs from his body.
stops.quote_source: Sentence of the visitador Jose Antonio de Areche, Cusco, 15 May 1781; English translation via en.wikipedia
suggested_refs: The Spanish original of Areche's sentence of 15 May 1781

stops.name: Cusco, Plaza de Armas, the eighteenth of May
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is brought into the square and made to watch. Tomasa Tito Condemayta dies, then his uncle Francisco Tupa Amaro, then his brother-in-law Antonio Bastidas, then his son Hipolito with his tongue cut out, then Micaela Bastidas, whose neck the garrote will not close on and who is finished with cords. Antonio Oblitas, who hanged the corregidor in November, dies here too. Then his own tongue is taken, and the horses are driven outward, and they cannot tear him apart, and the executioners come with knives.
stops.quote: atado a las colas de cuatro caballos que tirando en direcciones opuestas no pudieron descuartizarlo
stops.quote_source: Contemporary account of the execution, Cusco, 18 May 1781, quoted in es.wikipedia
suggested_refs: Areche's official account of the execution of 18 May 1781

segments.name: The Body Dispersed, the Name Forbidden

stops.name: Cusco, the ashes in the Watanay
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the disposal; the day follows the sequence given by es.wikipedia
stops.campa: The torso is carried to a hill above the city and burned, and the ashes are thrown into the Watanay, so that nothing is left to bury and nowhere is left to visit. This is deliberate and is stated as such in the order: no grave, no relic, no place anyone can go. Two centuries later there is still no tomb of Tupac Amaru II anywhere in Peru, only markers and a square. The horses failed at their part of the sentence in front of the whole city. This part of it, done quietly by a few men with a fire and a river, holds.
suggested_refs: The disposal order for the remains, and the hill above Cusco where the torso was burned

stops.name: Tinta, the head on the road
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the dispersal follows the execution within days. Individual arrival dates in each town are not recorded.
stops.campa: The head is shown in Cusco and then sent down to Tinta, the provincial capital where Arriaga kept his ledgers and where the whole thing began. It is set up where people going to market must pass it. The reasoning is legible: the towns that watched the corregidor hang will watch what the crown does to the man who hanged him, and in the same square. For the rest of that year the province is governed by what the people on the market road are made to walk past.
suggested_refs: The distribution order listing the towns to receive the remains

stops.name: Tungasuca, an arm at his own seat
stops.date_confidence: approximate: month only. The town is named in es.wikipedia; no arrival date is recorded.
stops.campa: One arm goes back to Tungasuca, to the village he governed for fourteen years, to the plaza where he issued the bando that freed the enslaved and where the corregidor was hanged before a crowd. His wife's orders went out from this seat to two provinces. The house stands empty now and the arm is set up in front of it. Of all the towns on the distribution list this one is chosen for what it will say rather than for how far it reaches. Nobody in the village needs the point explained.
suggested_refs: The Condorcanqui-Bastidas house at Tungasuca after the confiscations of 1781

stops.name: Ayapata, an arm sent east into Carabaya
stops.date_confidence: approximate: month only. es.wikipedia names the town but records no date.
stops.campa: The other arm travels east over the cordillera into Carabaya, the gold country on the edge of the forest, where the levies pan the rivers under the same draft that feeds Potosi. It is a long way to carry a piece of a man, and the distance is the point: the crown is drawing a perimeter with his body and wants the perimeter wide. Carabaya had risen with the rest, and Carabaya is to be shown what rising costs, at the far end of a road no army wants to march twice.
suggested_refs: Records of the gold levies of Carabaya and their part in the 1780 unrest

stops.name: Livitaca, the legs to the west
stops.date_confidence: approximate: month only. The towns are named in es.wikipedia without dates. Surimana, his birthplace, is not on the documented list, despite later accounts placing remains there.
stops.campa: One leg goes west to Livitaca in Chumbivilcas, the other south to Santa Rosa in Melgar, near the lake road he took in December. With the head at Tinta and the arms at Tungasuca and Ayapata, six towns hold a piece of him and no town holds enough to bury. The crown has performed an anatomy on the rebellion's own geography. What it does not anticipate is the story already told in these villages about a dismembered Inca who is slowly coming back together. That story has room for one more.
suggested_refs: Local memory at Livitaca and Santa Rosa of the 1781 exhibitions

stops.name: Cusco, the bando of Areche
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the decree follows the execution; the month is given, the day is not recorded
stops.campa: Areche then decrees what may not exist. Quechua is banned from official and public use. Indigenous dress is banned. Hereditary Inca titles and the nobility holding them are abolished. Portraits of the Inca rulers are to be taken down and destroyed, and the keeping of Inca genealogies is forbidden. In the same season the corregidor and the reparto are abolished too: the crown ends the abuses the rising named and ends the people who named them, and enters both in the same column as order restored.
suggested_refs: The full text of Areche's bando of 1781 banning Quechua, dress, titles and portraits

stops.name: La Paz, the siege of Tupac Katari
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the first siege of La Paz opens in March 1781 without a firm day in the reachable sources; the second runs 7 August to 17 October 1781
stops.campa: In Upper Peru, Julian Apaza takes the name Tupac Katari, joining the name of the Inca at Cusco to that of the Katari brothers of Chayanta, and closes on La Paz with his wife Bartolina Sisa and his sister Gregoria Apaza. The Aymara rising is allied to the Quechua one and organized apart from it, with its own leaders, its own grievances and its own council. Two sieges keep the city starving through the year. Reseguin breaks the second in October with ten thousand men.
suggested_refs: Aymara-language accounts of the sieges of La Paz, 1781

stops.name: Sicuani, the amnesty signed
stops.date_confidence: attested; the figure of thirty thousand accepting amnesty by February 1782 is a reported estimate, not a count
stops.campa: Diego Cristobal has kept the war alive for eight months since his cousin's execution. At Sicuani he comes to terms with Bishop Moscoso and Jose del Valle: a royal amnesty in exchange for laying down arms. Some thirty thousand are reported to accept it within weeks. The bishop who excommunicated Tupac Amaru II over Sangarara now stands as guarantor of the peace to his family, and the family, with no army left and a written pardon in hand, believes him. It is a document, and it is signed.
suggested_refs: The text of the Peace of Sicuani, 26 January 1782

stops.name: Marcapata, the amnesty broken
stops.date_confidence: attested; the arrest and the execution are four months and one province apart, not a single event as some summaries have it
stops.campa: Fourteen months into the peace, soldiers take Diego Cristobal at Marcapata, in the montane country east of Cusco, and take his whole household with him: his mother, his wife, the rest. The charge is conspiracy against the accords he himself signed. No source consulted shows the evidence for it. The pardon had been issued in the king's name and witnessed by a bishop, and it holds until the last Tupac Amaru is standing somewhere a garrison can reach him.
suggested_refs: The conspiracy charges laid against Diego Cristobal Tupac Amaru in 1783

stops.name: Cusco, the pincers
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Four months after Marcapata, in the same square, Diego Cristobal is torn with red-hot pincers, then hanged and quartered. His wife and his mother are executed with him. The surviving relatives are shipped to Spain and most of them die on the voyage. With this the line that claimed the Inca descent is finished as a political fact: there is no one left in the valleys to proclaim. The whole cycle has cost something near a hundred thousand lives, by estimates that vary with the historian.
suggested_refs: The passenger and mortality lists for the 1780s deportations of Tupac Amaru relatives to Spain

stops.name: Madrid, the last son
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the death date; the burial site is not identified, and the shipwreck that circulates in his story belongs to a different voyage carrying other relatives
stops.campa: Fernando was ten years old when they made him watch. He is sent toward Africa, escapes, is retaken and imprisoned at Cadiz, and dies in Madrid at twenty-seven, in the capital of the monarchy that killed his family. Some accounts put a shipwreck in the middle of that journey and some do not; the wreck usually named belongs to another ship carrying other relatives. Nobody records where in Madrid he lies. In 2025 remains described as symbolic are carried home to Peru.
sources: micaela_bastidas.journey.json (which carries the shipwreck this file does not)
suggested_refs: Madrid burial records for Fernando Tupac Amaru, died 30 July 1798

stops.name: Tucuman, the stolen house restored
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Thirty-five years after the square at Cusco, Manuel Belgrano stands before a congress at Tucuman and proposes that the new states restore the Inca dynasty and seat it again at Cusco: the stolen house restored. The delegates do not adopt it. But the proposal is made in a republican assembly, in earnest, as a constitutional option, and what it proposes is the argument Condorcanqui made with mules and levies and a presumed manifesto, and lost. His claim outlives his body and arrives in a room full of lawyers.
suggested_refs: The minutes of the Congress of Tucuman for 6 July 1816

stops.name: Lima, the effigy in the Panteon
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the Panteon de los Proceres was dedicated in 1924, but the installation date of his effigy is not given in any source reached
stops.campa: In the Panteon de los Proceres he stands among the founders of the republic, beside Micaela Bastidas. Twenty-four of the honored lie in the crypt below in their coffins. He is not among them and neither is she. They are effigies, because there is nothing to inter: the ashes went into the Watanay in 1781 so that this room, whenever it came to be built, would have nothing to put in it. The sentence is still being enforced inside the monument raised to its victim.
suggested_refs: The installation record of the Tupac Amaru II and Micaela Bastidas effigies in the Panteon

stops.name: Montevideo, the name crosses the continent
stops.date_confidence: approximate: leaflets under a related slogan appear in November 1964, and the name is claimed for an action in August 1965; the day is not fixed
stops.campa: An urban movement in Uruguay, two thousand miles from Canas and with no organizational descent from anything he founded, calls itself the Tupamaros. The name travels on its own now, cut loose from the mule roads and the alcabala, and it means refusal of an order imposed from outside. A Venezuelan party will take it later, and a Peruvian one. Nobody borrows his program, which was local and specific and mostly about taxes. They borrow the fact that he said no.
suggested_refs: MLN-Tupamaros founding documents on the choice of the name

stops.name: Lima, the hall renamed
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the national-hero designation and the agrarian reform fall in 1969, the renaming of the hall in 1972, and no day is given for either
stops.campa: A military government in Lima makes him the emblem of its land reform and puts his face on the currency, and in the government palace it takes down the portrait of Francisco Pizarro and renames the Salon Pizarro for him. The room where the conquest was honored now carries the name of the man the conquest's heirs quartered. A later president, unimpressed by the arithmetic, takes to calling it Tupac Pizarro. The state that killed him has become a state that requires him.
suggested_refs: The 1969 decree naming Tupac Amaru II a national hero, distinct from the 1972 renaming

stops.name: Lima, the residence on the hill
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement, formed in Peru in the early 1980s under his name and his face, seizes the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima with hundreds of hostages inside. The siege runs four months and ends with a tunnel and a shooting, and with the organization finished. The name has now been carried by a colonial rebel, a military junta and a guerrilla group the junta's successors destroy: three claims on one man, made in one city, inside thirty years.
suggested_refs: MRTA statements on the adoption of the name and image of Tupac Amaru II

stops.name: Surimana, the body underground
stops.date_confidence: oral tradition, undatable: the Inkarri cycle was recorded by twentieth-century folklorists and is older than its attachment to him. The date is a placeholder for a story with no date, set late so the stop reads last; it asserts nothing about when the tradition arose.
stops.campa: In the villages there is a story older than he is: that the body of a killed Inca lies scattered underground and is slowly growing back together, head to trunk to limbs, and that when it is whole again the world will turn over and be set right. It was told before 1781 and it did not need him. But the crown had just cut a man into six pieces and sent them to six towns, and the story was standing there ready, and it took him. He is the body under the ground now, and the ground is patient.
sources: Inkarri accounts collected by Jose Maria Arguedas, at second hand
suggested_refs: Arguedas's collected Inkarri testimonies and their variants naming Tupac Amaru II
